Planes Over Bartlett — Live

Each dot on the chart is a real plane. Its place on the chart matches its direction and distance from home, so you can look up and check.

✓ How to verify this with your own eyes

  1. Find plane #1 in the list below — it is the nearest or most interesting.
  2. Read its big gold line. Once the live list below loads, plane #1's own gold line will be copied here word for word — the same live distance and the same live direction, from the same stored values — so you can check it without scrolling. Until then this step shows no distance and no direction, on purpose: a made-up example here could send you looking the wrong way.
  3. Step outside, face that compass direction, and look up at about the height given. A high plane leaves a white trail on a clear day; a low one you may hear first.
  4. Check the feed time below. If it says the feed is several minutes old, the plane has moved on — tap REFRESH.

Your neighborhood airports

What am I likely to see?

FedEx freighters, day and night. Memphis is home to the FedEx Express World Hub. The biggest rush arrives late at night, roughly 10 p.m. to 1 a.m.

Airliners overhead on routes into Memphis International, about 14 miles southwest.

Military visitors at Millington, just north. Small planes from Baker and DeWitt Spain on pretty days.

Live aircraft: adsb.fi open data (v3), personal family use, read first from a same-origin cached feed (aircraft.json) refreshed on a schedule — the same pattern most personal ADS-B dashboards use, because the community feeds send no CORS headers for direct browser reading. Public relays are only a backup. Positions come from aircraft radio broadcasts (ADS-B) heard by volunteer receivers — coverage is not complete, and some military, government and privacy-blocked aircraft never appear. The feed's dst distance is in nautical miles; Orbit converts it to statute miles (×1.15078) for display, and also checks it from the plane's latitude and longitude.

Tracker · Satellites

The Space Station, Live

The gold dot on the world map is the station right now. The star is Bartlett. Watch the dot move — it crosses the whole map in about 45 minutes.

Getting the station's position…
● gold = Space Station★ = Bartlett, TennesseeDashed line = its path aheadDark side = night on Earth

Getting the station's place…

Over (nearest place)—
Coordinates—
Height above Earth—
Speed—
Sunlight—
People aboardCrewed — Orbit shows no number without a live source
Updated—
Distance from Bartlett (across the ground)—
Direction from Bartlett—

To verify: when the distance above is under about 1,200 miles and the station is in sunlight just after sunset, it can be visible from Bartlett as a bright, steady light. Otherwise it is too far or in daylight — the map position is still exact. In plain terms: about 260 miles up — Bartlett to St. Louis, straight up — at 17,500 mph, crossing the U.S. in about 10 minutes.

🛰 When will it pass over Bartlett?

The station circles Earth every 93 minutes, so it passes over Bartlett several times a day — but you can only see it when three things line up:

  1. It is dark where you are — just after sunset or just before sunrise are the good windows.
  2. The station itself is still in sunlight up there, shining against the dark sky.
  3. It passes close enough — the “Distance from Bartlett” above reads under about 1,200 miles, and the sky is clear.

Exact pass times shift a little every day as the orbit drifts, so Orbit doesn't print a timetable that could quietly go stale. Instead, on a clear evening, watch the live distance above: when it starts falling toward a few hundred miles in the hour after sunset, a bright pass is coming — step out and look for a steady, non-blinking white light crossing the sky. On a cloudy or foggy night it stays hidden, however close it passes.

Other satellites worth knowing

Hubble Space Telescope

Orbiting about 320 miles up since 1990, Hubble gave us our deepest views of the universe.

Tiangong — China's space station

A second crewed station, a little smaller than the ISS, with its own crew aboard.

Weather satellites (NOAA & GOES)

22,000 miles up, GOES-East watches Bartlett's weather all day and takes the satellite pictures on the news.

Starlink "trains"

For a few days after a launch, new Starlink satellites travel in a line, like a string of pearls in the twilight sky.

Live ISS position: wheretheiss.at, from NORAD orbital data (CelesTrak). Crew: the station is crewed and has been continuously occupied since November 2, 2000 — Orbit deliberately shows no crew number, because the free crew feeds available to a browser page are stale or insecure, and a wrong number presented as live would be worse than none. Place names on the map are the nearest large region, worked out from the coordinates — over oceans, the ocean's name is the honest answer.

How to read the labels

LIVE  Measured right now from a live feed.

CALCULATED  Worked out from the spacecraft's known path. There is no GPS in deep space; NASA calculates these, and so do we — honestly labeled.

STILL FLYING  Still in service today, but with no live position feed here.

MISSION RECORD  A completed mission, from the official record.

Help & Settings

Make It Yours

Text size

Make the words on every page bigger — headings, labels and small print included.

On the website copy of Orbit (the one at aubreyhayes47.github.io/orbit-360), this setting — and your Read to Me voice speed — are remembered on this device, so they're still set when you come back. In some in-app copies the settings last while the page is open; if your text size has reset, it takes one tap to set it again.

How to use Orbit 360

1. The home page is a dashboard: what's overhead right now, tonight's verdict, and one story.

2. Tap ⌂ HOME at the top of any page to come back.

3. Tap ▶ READ TO ME to hear a page read aloud. ■ STOP stops it. Speed switches between Normal and Slower (remembered on the website copy, like text size).

4½. Seeing the Space Station: it passes over Bartlett several times a day, but it's only visible just after sunset or before sunrise, when it's still in sunlight, passes within about 1,200 miles, and the sky is clear. The Station page explains this in full — pass times shift daily, so Orbit shows the live distance to watch instead of a timetable that could go stale.

4. On the sky chart, a plane's dot sits in its real direction and distance from Bartlett — step outside, face that way, and look up.

5. LIVE means measured just now. CALCULATED means worked out from a known path.

Put Orbit on the Home Screen

On an iPhone: open this page in Safari, tap Share (square with an up arrow), then Add to Home Screen. Orbit then opens full-screen from its own icon, like an app — no account or login, ever.

On Android: open in Chrome, tap ⋮, then Add to Home screen.

About the information

Space facts checked against NASA/JPL, November 7, 2026. Weather live from the National Weather Service. Station position live from orbital data. Airplane positions live from adsb.fi's open feed, read first from a cached copy on this same site (aircraft.json) because the feed does not answer browsers directly — that cached-feed pattern is what most small personal trackers use. Orbit shows the feed's name, its time, and how old it is on every report, and never shows an old report as live. Weather is from the National Weather Service first, with Open-Meteo as a labelled backup. No location is tracked — Local Sky always looks at Bartlett.
